docs.title: Deadlines, Budgets and Fail-Fast Guardrails
docs.text:
Guardrails are opt-in. Their defaults preserve normal completion-order, retry, streaming, token-accounting, and cancellation behavior.

from llm_minder import AbortMode, ErrorCategory, GuardrailConfig, ProcessorConfig

config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=20,
    attempt_timeout=30,
    guardrails=GuardrailConfig(
        total_timeout_per_item=180,
        batch_timeout=3600,
        abort_on_error_categories=frozenset({
            ErrorCategory.AUTHENTICATION,
            ErrorCategory.INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE,
        }),
        abort_mode=AbortMode.DRAIN_ACTIVE,
    ),
)

Timeouts must be finite numbers (not booleans) greater than zero, or None. All deadline calculations use a monotonic clock.

docs.title: Per-attempt timeout versus total item deadline
docs.text:
ProcessorConfig.attempt_timeout retains its existing meaning: it limits one strategy.execute() attempt after provider-capacity admission. Retries can each receive another attempt timeout.

GuardrailConfig.total_timeout_per_item is one end-to-end logical-item budget. It starts when execution of an accepted item begins and includes:

  • coordinated cooldown and startup-ramp waits;
  • pre-execution middleware and strategy error callbacks;
  • proactive rate-limiter waits;
  • provider-capacity admission;
  • every provider attempt;
  • retry cooldowns and backoff.

Every wait is bounded by the remaining budget. A provider call receives the lower of attempt_timeout and the remaining total budget, and no retry or new provider attempt starts after expiry. Completed-attempt timing and token usage remain on the terminal result.

Postprocessing and artifact persistence occur after the logical provider execution pipeline and are not included in the total item deadline. They have their own timeout/durability semantics. The queue wait before a worker picks up an item is also outside the item deadline; use batch_timeout to bound the whole run. In LLMCallPool, the pool semaphore wait is outside the executor's item deadline; use submit_timeout when the caller needs one budget that also includes pool admission.

Total expiry is terminal and non-retryable:

  • exception: ItemDeadlineExceeded;
  • error_category: framework_total_item_timeout.

A per-attempt attempt_timeout expiry is distinct: it is retryable, with error_category="framework_timeout" and timing.timeout_category="framework_execution_timeout". Put framework_timeout, not framework_execution_timeout, in abort_on_error_categories.

timing.timeout_category records where the time ran out (see TimeoutCategory for the values). A deadline reached while the item waited for provider capacity is admission_timeout, for both item and batch deadlines. The elapsed capacity wait still counts toward admission_wait_seconds, and it's kept when an abort ends the wait too.

docs.title: Batch deadlines
docs.text:
batch_timeout starts when process_all() or streaming execution starts, not when a processor object is constructed. At expiry, source consumption stops, no new provider attempt starts, and every already accepted item receives one terminal result. Work not yet pulled from an async source was never accepted and is not materialized.

Queued or interrupted collateral items use BatchDeadlineExceeded and error_category="batch_deadline_exceeded". process_all() and process_prompts() return completed and collateral results with result.termination.kind == "batch_timeout". process_stream() yields all terminal results for accepted work and then ends normally. Low-level streaming callers can inspect processor.termination after completion.

The abort mode controls provider calls already in flight:

  • AbortMode.DRAIN_ACTIVE: let a provider call already registered as active finish, but do not start another retry or provider call afterward.
  • AbortMode.CANCEL_ACTIVE: cancel active provider calls and convert unfinished accepted work into batch-deadline results.

External caller cancellation is different: it still propagates after worker, producer, queue, and strategy cleanup and is not mislabeled as a deadline.

docs.title: Configurable fail-fast
docs.text:
abort_on_error_categories is empty by default. Use ErrorCategory members for the built-in categories (see the full list); plain strings, including categories returned by a custom classifier, work too. A configured category trips the shared abort controller only after an item reaches terminal failure; an intermediate retryable attempt does not abort a batch that could still recover. The first concurrent trigger wins and records its category and item ID.

Already completed results are preserved. Queued accepted items do not call the provider and receive BatchAbortedError with error_category="batch_aborted". The active-call behavior follows the same abort_mode described above. The returned batch reports termination.kind == "fail_fast".

LLMCallPool honours the same setting. The first request that finishes failed in a configured category stops the pool: later submits, including those waiting for a slot, return batch_aborted without calling the provider, and pool.termination reports why. The pool stays stopped until you call pool.resume(), so your code decides: fix the cause (re-authenticate, top up credit) and resume, or leave it stopped and shut down. Calls that started before a resume can't stop the resumed pool; a new failure in a configured category stops it again. call() and call_result() run one request, so the setting has nothing to stop there.

from llm_minder import ErrorCategory, GuardrailConfig, LLMCallPool, ProcessorConfig

config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=5,
    guardrails=GuardrailConfig(
        abort_on_error_categories=frozenset({ErrorCategory.AUTHENTICATION}),
    ),
)
async with LLMCallPool(strategy, config=config) as pool:
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(pool.submit_result(p) for p in prompts))
    if pool.termination is not None:
        print(pool.termination.reason)  # names the item, category and hint
        if credentials_refreshed():  # your own check
            pool.resume()

Choose categories that indicate a batch-wide condition. Good candidates when your provider classifier supplies reliable status information include:

  • ErrorCategory.AUTHENTICATION (HTTP 401, or expired or missing Google credentials);
  • ErrorCategory.PERMISSION_DENIED (HTTP 403), when permission is account/model-wide; and
  • ErrorCategory.INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE.

Depending on your setup, these are also batch-wide:

  • ErrorCategory.QUOTA_EXHAUSTED (Gemini daily quota);
  • ErrorCategory.TOKEN_ESTIMATOR_REQUIRED and ErrorCategory.QUOTA_SCOPE_ERROR (configuration failures that affect every item).

Do not use client_error as a blanket default: malformed input or validation can be item-specific. The provider-neutral classifier does not invent auth or permission categories when reliable status data is unavailable.

docs.title: Token and cost budgets
docs.text:
max_total_tokens and max_total_cost cap what one processor run spends. Both are opt-in soft caps.

Provisional: this API is new in v0.27 and may change in a minor release; see API stability.

from llm_minder import AttemptUsage, GuardrailConfig, ProcessorConfig

def price(usage: AttemptUsage) -> float:
    # Your prices, in your currency. llm-minder ships no price table.
    return (
        usage.usage.get("input_tokens", 0) * 0.15
        + usage.usage.get("output_tokens", 0) * 0.60
    ) / 1_000_000

config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=20,
    guardrails=GuardrailConfig(
        max_total_tokens=5_000_000,
        max_total_cost=25.0,
        cost_function=price,
    ),
)

What counts. Every physical provider attempt whose usage the provider reported, success or failure, including retries and rate-limited tries. Usage is counted as each attempt finishes, from the same observation that tokens-per-minute admission reconciles. These are not counted:

  • replayed results;
  • dry-run calls;
  • attempts that never started a provider call;
  • attempts whose usage the provider didn't report (they appear in budget_unknown_usage_attempts);
  • usage a strategy adds only later, from on_error.

So the budget can be lower than a result's token_usage.

Reaching a cap. When the total reaches a cap (equality counts), the run stops like a batch deadline, with termination.kind == "budget_exceeded":

  • no new provider call or retry starts;
  • abort_mode decides whether calls already running drain or are cancelled;
  • accepted items that didn't finish receive BatchBudgetExceeded with error_category="batch_budget_exceeded".

The attempt that reached the cap keeps its outcome if it succeeded. If it failed, its result becomes batch_budget_exceeded, with the provider error kept as the exception's __context__.

Overshoot. Final usage can exceed the cap by the usage of the attempt that reached it plus other attempts that had already started, which is at most max_workers attempts in total. There is no numeric bound unless each attempt's usage is bounded, for example with max_tokens. With max_workers=1 and a cap of 10 tokens, a single call that reports 100 overshoots by 90. Providers may still bill calls that AbortMode.CANCEL_ACTIVE cancels.

Cost function. max_total_cost requires cost_function, which is called once per attempt with known usage. It receives an AttemptUsage: the item ID, attempt and try numbers, the strategy, a read-only copy of the token usage, and whether the call succeeded. Pass the strategy to price model escalation per attempt.

  • It must be synchronous and fast: it runs on the event loop, and a blocking call can't be interrupted.
  • It must return a finite, non-negative number.
  • If it raises or returns anything else (including an awaitable or a bool), the run stops with budget_exceeded, tokens are still counted, and budget_cost_complete becomes False. Its exception message is not logged.
  • A cost_function without max_total_cost only tracks cost.

Reporting. await processor.get_stats() adds budget_tokens_used, budget_cost_used, budget_cost_complete, and budget_unknown_usage_attempts when a budget or cost function is configured. The termination reason names the cap and the amount used.

Scope. Budgets apply to processor runs (process_all(), streaming, process_prompts(), process_stream()). call(), call_result(), and LLMCallPool reject them with ValueError rather than ignoring a safety cap. Every run starts with a fresh budget, including a resumed run.

Artifacts. batch_budget_exceeded results are audit records like other batch-abort results: written best-effort and never replayed. A BatchResult serialized with termination.kind == "budget_exceeded" can't be read by v0.26 or earlier.

docs.title: Provider call cap
docs.text:
max_total_tokens and max_total_cost are soft caps, because usage is only known after a call finishes. When a run must not make more than a set number of calls, for example a paid run approved for "at most 500 calls", use max_provider_calls:

config = ProcessorConfig(guardrails=GuardrailConfig(max_provider_calls=500))
  • Every physical provider attempt counts: first tries, retries, and rate-limit retries. Replayed results don't.
  • The count is checked and taken before each call starts, in one step, so concurrent workers can't overshoot it. An attempt that is admitted but stopped before reaching the provider, for example by its item deadline, gives its call back.
  • A run whose items all finish within the cap completes normally. Once the cap is used up, the next attempt that needs a call is refused, and the run stops exactly like a token or cost budget: termination.kind == "budget_exceeded", a reason of Provider call cap reached: 500 of 500 calls started, and batch_budget_exceeded for the refused item and for unstarted items. abort_mode decides what happens to calls already running.
  • await processor.get_stats() reports provider_calls_started.
  • Like budgets, the cap applies to processor runs only; call(), call_result() and LLMCallPool reject it. It can be combined with max_total_tokens and max_total_cost; whichever trips first stops the run.

The cap counts calls the framework makes. An SDK that retries HTTP requests internally can bill more than one request per call. The built-in OpenAI-compatible models pass max_retries=0 to the SDK by default. If you build the client yourself, or use Gemini's own retry options, turn those retries off for a strict cap.

docs.title: Attempt admission hook
docs.text:
Provisional: new in 1.2; it may change in a minor release.

max_total_cost is a soft cap: usage is known only after a call finishes, so calls already running can take a run past it. When a run must never pass a limit, for example "this run may spend at most $20", reserve each call's worst case before it starts and settle to its actual cost afterwards. GuardrailConfig(admission=...) takes an object with two synchronous methods, admit(request) and settle(ticket, usage, success) (the AttemptAdmission protocol):

  • admit(request) runs immediately before each physical provider attempt (first tries, retries and rate-limit retries), after every other gate: provider capacity, cooldowns, RPM/TPM admission and the max_provider_calls check. A ticket is never held while an attempt waits. It returns a ticket, any object, or raises AdmissionRefused to refuse.
  • settle(ticket, usage, success) is called exactly once for every ticket admit returned: after a success, a provider failure, a timeout, a cancellation or an abort, and also when the attempt was admitted but never reached the provider (for example its item deadline expired, or a cooldown began). usage is the attempt's TokenUsage, including usage attached to a failed attempt's exception. An attempt that never reached the provider settles with zero usage (input_tokens, output_tokens and total_tokens all 0), since nothing was sent. None means a call started but no usage is known, for example it timed out or was cancelled; a provider may still bill it.

The processor calls both methods on the event loop, outside its own locks, with no await between admit and the start of the call. So a hook that checks and reserves against its own in-memory state is atomic without a lock. That's why both must be synchronous and must not block: GuardrailConfig rejects async def methods, and a hook that needs I/O should reserve in memory and reconcile elsewhere.

The request. AttemptRequest carries item_id, attempt (the logical attempt, as passed to execute()), try_number (the physical try; a rate-limit retry keeps attempt and gets a new try_number), the strategy, and what the call will send:

  • prompt for a string item, or messages for a message-list item. Exactly one is set (prompt is "" for a message-list item), so an estimator must read whichever one is.
  • generation_config: for a ModelStrategy, the effective config for this attempt, with attempt_generation_config() merged over generation_config, so the output bound (max_tokens, max_output_tokens) is visible. None when the strategy has none, and for other strategies. Building it calls attempt_generation_config() a second time per attempt, so keep that method free of side effects.

The request doesn't include a system instruction or tools set on the model, so leave a margin for them.

Refusal. AdmissionRefused, or any other exception from admit, stops the run like a budget: no new provider call or retry starts, abort_mode decides what happens to calls already running, and termination.kind == "admission_refused" with the exception's message as the reason (another exception type is also logged, and its reason names the type). The refused item and every accepted item that hadn't finished end with AdmissionRefused and error_category="batch_admission_refused". A refused attempt isn't retried, isn't classified as a provider error, and isn't counted in provider_calls_started.

A failing settle. An exception from settle is logged and stops the run the same way, as admission_refused: a spend cap that can't record spend must not keep admitting. The attempt that was being settled keeps its own outcome.

Scope and artifacts. Like budgets, the hook applies to processor runs only; call(), call_result() and LLMCallPool reject GuardrailConfig(admission=...) with ValueError. batch_admission_refused results are audit records like other batch-abort results, in both artifact stores: written best-effort and never replayed, so a resumed run executes those items again. A BatchResult serialized with termination.kind == "admission_refused" can't be read by 1.1 or earlier.

SDK retries. The hook sees the attempts the framework makes. An SDK that retries HTTP requests inside one attempt can bill several requests for one ticket. The built-in OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic models build their clients with max_retries=0. With admission set, the processor logs a warning, once per model, when a built-in model's client retries on its own: a max_retries override, a client you passed in, or Gemini retry_options.

docs.title: Example: a hard spend cap
docs.text:
The cap below reserves input_estimate * input_price + max_output * output_price at admit, refuses when committed plus reserved spend would pass the limit, and settles each ticket to the attempt's actual cost. The input estimate counts UTF-8 bytes, which can't be fewer than the tokens a byte-level tokenizer produces, so it is high (about four times, for English) but safe. For Anthropic prompt caching the worst case prices every input token as a cache write (cache_write_rate 1.25 for the 5-minute TTL, 2.0 for the 1-hour TTL), and the settled cost charges cache reads at the discounted rate. The built-in models report input_tokens including cache reads and writes, which is what actual_cost assumes.

import json
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass

from llm_minder import (
    AdmissionRefused,
    AttemptRequest,
    CachedTokenRates,
    GuardrailConfig,
    ProcessorConfig,
    TokenUsage,
)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Prices:
    input_per_mtok: float
    output_per_mtok: float
    cache_read_rate: float = 1.0  # fraction of the input price for a cache read
    cache_write_rate: float = 1.0  # multiple of the input price for a cache write


class HardSpendCap:
    """Committed plus reserved spend never passes ``limit``."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        limit: float,
        prices: Prices,
        *,
        default_max_output: int,
        overhead_tokens: int = 2_000,
    ) -> None:
        self.limit = limit
        self.prices = prices
        self.default_max_output = default_max_output  # when the config sets no bound
        self.overhead_tokens = overhead_tokens  # system instruction, tools, formatting
        self.spent = 0.0  # settled cost
        self.reserved = 0.0  # worst case of admitted attempts not yet settled

    def input_estimate(self, request: AttemptRequest) -> int:
        if request.messages is None:
            text = request.prompt
        else:
            text = json.dumps([dict(message) for message in request.messages], default=str)
        return len(text.encode("utf-8")) + self.overhead_tokens

    def max_output(self, request: AttemptRequest) -> int:
        # Providers differ in which alias wins when several are set, so take the
        # largest. A bound that isn't a positive int can't be trusted to apply,
        # so it brings back the default rather than shrinking the reservation.
        config = request.generation_config or {}
        keys = ("max_tokens", "max_output_tokens", "max_completion_tokens")
        bounds: list[int] = []
        for key in (k for k in keys if k in config):
            value = config[key]
            valid = isinstance(value, int) and not isinstance(value, bool) and value > 0
            bounds.append(value if valid else self.default_max_output)
        return max(bounds, default=self.default_max_output)

    def admit(self, request: AttemptRequest) -> float:
        p = self.prices
        input_price = p.input_per_mtok * max(1.0, p.cache_write_rate)
        worst = (
            self.input_estimate(request) * input_price
            + self.max_output(request) * p.output_per_mtok
        ) / 1_000_000
        if self.spent + self.reserved + worst > self.limit:
            raise AdmissionRefused(
                f"Spend cap ${self.limit:.2f}: ${self.spent:.4f} spent and "
                f"${self.reserved:.4f} reserved; the next attempt could cost ${worst:.4f}"
            )
        self.reserved += worst
        return worst  # the ticket

    def settle(self, ticket: object, usage: TokenUsage | None, success: bool) -> None:
        assert isinstance(ticket, float)
        self.reserved -= ticket
        # Unknown usage may still have been billed (a timeout or cancellation),
        # so a hard cap keeps the worst case.
        self.spent += ticket if usage is None else self.actual_cost(usage)

    def actual_cost(self, usage: TokenUsage) -> float:
        p = self.prices
        read = usage.get("cached_input_tokens", 0)
        written = usage.get("cache_write_input_tokens", 0)
        plain = max(0, usage.get("input_tokens", 0) - read - written)
        input_tokens = plain + read * p.cache_read_rate + written * p.cache_write_rate
        output_cost = usage.get("output_tokens", 0) * p.output_per_mtok
        return (input_tokens * p.input_per_mtok + output_cost) / 1_000_000


cap = HardSpendCap(
    20.0,
    # Placeholder prices per million tokens: use your model's price list.
    Prices(
        input_per_mtok=3.0,
        output_per_mtok=15.0,
        cache_read_rate=CachedTokenRates.ANTHROPIC_READ,
        cache_write_rate=CachedTokenRates.ANTHROPIC_WRITE,  # ANTHROPIC_WRITE_1H for 1-hour
    ),
    default_max_output=16_000,  # AnthropicModel's default max_tokens
)
config = ProcessorConfig(guardrails=GuardrailConfig(admission=cap))

After the run, cap.spent is the settled spend. Keeping the worst case for usage=None makes the cap strict, at the price of charging started calls that failed before billing (a refused connection, a 429 or 5xx response with no usage) at their worst case. Attempts that never started settle with zero usage, so they release their reservation exactly. Release the reservation for None instead if you'd rather under-count those than over-count them. Without caching, leave both cache rates at 1.0.

docs.title: Cache hit-rate floor
docs.text:
A prompt cache that stops hitting can multiply a run's input cost without any call failing. Every processor run counts cache reads and writes per cache group, and min_cache_hit_rate stops the run when a group's recent hit rate falls below a floor. This section is the reference; Prompt caching is the how-to, including which providers support what and how to choose the values.

Provisional: new in 0.30; it may change in a minor release.

from llm_minder import GuardrailConfig, ProcessorConfig

config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=20,
    guardrails=GuardrailConfig(
        min_cache_hit_rate=0.8,  # None (the default) turns the floor off
        cache_hit_window=50,     # measured calls per group in the sliding window
    ),
)

Groups. An attempt's group is the cache_group key in its metadata:

  • Every built-in model takes a cache_group="..." label, and a call can override it with config={"cache_group": "..."}. The label is never sent to the provider, and it wins over the defaults below.
  • OpenAI-compatible models (OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek) use the request's prompt_cache_key if one is set (including one from the model's prompt_cache_key option, see OpenAI prompt caching), else si: plus a 12-character hash of the system instruction.
  • GeminiModel uses the system-instruction hash. GeminiCachedModel uses gemini-cache: plus a hash of the cached content, which stays the same when the cache is renewed.
  • A cache_group key from a metadata_extractors entry wins over all of these.
  • PydanticAIStrategy sets no group. CallableStrategy and custom strategies can set metadata["cache_group"] themselves.
  • Attempts without a group are counted together as the None group.

A group longer than 128 characters is replaced by its SHA-256. A run tracks at most 64 groups; attempts for further groups are counted together in cache_groups_overflow, with one warning.

What counts. Provider attempts in this run that returned a result. Failed attempts, replayed results and dry-run calls aren't counted. An attempt is measured when its usage is known and reports positive input tokens; others are counted as unmeasured_calls and never move the rate.

The floor. Each group keeps a window of its last cache_hit_window measured attempts. Once a group's window is full, a window hit rate (cached input tokens over input tokens) below min_cache_hit_rate stops the run like configurable fail-fast: termination.kind == "fail_fast", termination.error_category == "cache_hit_rate_below_floor", abort_mode applies, and items that hadn't started end batch_aborted. The window is also the warm-up, and each group has its own, so a group's first cache writes aren't held against it. With a floor configured, a 65th group also stops the run, since the floor can't be enforced for groups it doesn't track. If the same attempt reaches a token or cost budget, the run ends budget_exceeded instead.

Miss reasons. A strategy can put a provider's explanation of a miss in metadata["cache_miss_reason"] (a string, kept to 64 characters). Each group reports its latest one as last_miss_reason, and the floor's stop reason ends with it. OpenAI's Responses API models set it from prompt_cache_diagnostics when the response carries a cache-miss diagnosis.

Reporting. await processor.get_stats() and the BATCH_COMPLETED event carry cache_groups, a list sorted by input tokens, and cache_groups_overflow (None unless there was overflow). Each entry has group, measured_calls, unmeasured_calls, input_tokens, cached_input_tokens, cache_write_input_tokens, hit_rate (cumulative), window_hit_rate (over the last cache_hit_window measured calls, None until the window is full) and last_miss_reason. BatchResult has no per-group view: results include replays and add up retries, which isn't what the floor measures.

Scope. Processor runs only. call(), call_result() and LLMCallPool reject min_cache_hit_rate with ValueError. A resumed run starts with fresh counts.

Call pools. LLMCallPool keeps the same per-group statistics without a floor. pool.cache_stats() returns cache_groups and cache_groups_overflow in the same shape, counted since the pool was created or last reset, and every group includes window_hit_rate over its last cache_hit_window measured calls. A long-lived pool's cumulative hit_rate moves slowly, so the window shows a recent drop. pool.reset_cache_stats() clears everything, including the 64-group cap; a call still running at the reset is counted when it returns. Both methods are synchronous, so call them from the pool's event loop. call() and call_result() keep no statistics.

Your own tracker. CacheGroupTracker (provisional) is the accounting behind all of this, with the same rule for what counts and the same window check as the floor. pool.cache_tracker is the pool's live one. Use it to carry a pool's statistics across a restart, or to apply a floor where the processor can't:

import json

from llm_minder import CacheGroupTracker, LLMCallPool

# On startup: continue the saved statistics, if any.
tracker = CacheGroupTracker.from_dict(json.loads(saved)) if saved else None
pool = LLMCallPool(strategy, config=config, cache_tracker=tracker)

# Between calls: apply a floor yourself.
for breach in pool.cache_tracker.below_floor(0.8):
    logger.warning(breach.message)

# At a checkpoint or on shutdown: save the exact state.
saved = json.dumps(pool.cache_tracker.to_dict())
  • record(group, usage, miss_reason=None) counts one call; record_result(result) counts a WorkItemResult from its metadata and token_usage, skipping failures.
  • stats() returns cache_groups and cache_groups_overflow in the shape above.
  • below_floor(floor) returns a CacheFloorBreach for each group whose full window is below floor (lowest first) and one with overflow=True if more than 64 groups were seen. Each breach's message is the stop reason a processor run would report.
  • to_dict() returns JSON-serializable state, every group's window included, and CacheGroupTracker.from_dict() restores it exactly (it raises ValueError on bad data). A pool given a restored tracker uses the tracker's window, not cache_hit_window.

Without saved state, you can rebuild a tracker by feeding it saved results with record_result. It reads lower than the live tracker did when retries were billed: a result's token_usage adds up every attempt of its item, failed ones included, whereas live tracking counts only the attempt that returned. A processor run always starts with a fresh tracker; it doesn't take a saved one.

docs.title: End-to-end checkpointed run
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from llm_minder import (
    AbortMode,
    ArtifactIdentity,
    ErrorCategory,
    GuardrailConfig,
    JsonlArtifactStore,
    ProcessorConfig,
    ResumePolicy,
    process_prompts,
)

store = JsonlArtifactStore(
    "run.jsonl",
    identity=ArtifactIdentity(
        provider="openai",
        model="example-model",
        prompt_version="invoice-v4",
        parser_version="invoice-schema-v2",
        application_version="billing-pipeline-v7",
    ),
)

config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=20,
    attempt_timeout=30,
    guardrails=GuardrailConfig(
        total_timeout_per_item=180,
        batch_timeout=3600,
        abort_on_error_categories=frozenset({
            ErrorCategory.AUTHENTICATION,
            ErrorCategory.INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE,
        }),

        abort_mode=AbortMode.DRAIN_ACTIVE,
    ),
)

result = await process_prompts(
    strategy,
    prompts,
    config=config,
    artifact_store=store,
    resume=ResumePolicy.REUSE_SUCCESSES,
    preserve_order=True,
)

Path("summary.json").write_text(result.to_json(), encoding="utf-8")

Serialization, artifact I/O, and programming failures remain exceptions. They are not disguised as controlled guardrail termination.

docs.title: Retry delay cannot fit
docs.text: If the actual jittered retry delay is at least the remaining item deadline, llm-minder fails immediately with ItemDeadlineExceeded instead of spending that time waiting. Its message and cause retain the last provider error; the attempt timing keeps that error's category and reports zero retry-backoff wait. The final result uses framework_total_item_timeout, so abort_on_error_categories matches that final category rather than the provider category. The existing guardrail audit and non-replayable-record behavior remains in effect.

docs.title: Large Runs (100k–1M items)
docs.text: How to run six or seven digits of work items with bounded memory, restart safety, and evidence instead of hope. This page assumes the concepts in Bounded Work and Backpressure and Results, Artifacts, and Resume.

docs.title: Stream, don't collect
docs.text:
process_prompts() retains every terminal result in its returned BatchResult — at large scale that is deliberate collection, not bounded memory. For large runs use process_stream() with a lazy source and consume each result as it arrives:

from llm_minder import (
    ProcessorConfig,
    ResumePolicy,
    SqliteArtifactStore,
    process_stream,
)

async def source():
    async for row in database.cursor("SELECT id, prompt FROM work"):
        yield row.id, row.prompt          # never materialize the full input

config = ProcessorConfig(
    concurrency=64,
    max_queue_size=512,          # input backpressure: producer blocks when full
    max_result_queue_size=512,   # result backpressure: workers pause for a slow sink
)

store = SqliteArtifactStore("runs/big-run.sqlite")
async for item in process_stream(
    strategy,
    source(),
    config=config,
    artifact_store=store,
    resume=ResumePolicy.REUSE_SUCCESSES,
):
    await sink(item)                      # keep aggregates, not the item list

An async sink that writes downstream (database, queue, file) should hold aggregates and counters, not accumulate WorkItemResult objects.

docs.title: Sizing the knobs
docs.text:
• concurrency sizes workers, provider admission, and built-in connection pools together. Start at 32–64 for fake-fast or high-quota endpoints, 5–10 for ordinary rate-limited APIs, and let Choosing Your Limits guide refinement.
  • max_queue_size bounds accepted-but-unstarted items. A few multiples of concurrency (e.g. 512 for 64 workers) keeps workers fed while capping producer read-ahead.
  • max_result_queue_size bounds completed results awaiting your sink. Size it for your sink's burst tolerance; workers pause when it is full.

Bounded queues cap the queued objects. Active workers each hold one item, and your sink holds the result it is processing — the true in-flight ceiling is roughly max_queue_size + concurrency + max_result_queue_size + 1.

Watch the exact high-water marks in get_stats() to see how much of each bound a real run actually used.

docs.title: Choose SQLite for restartable scale
docs.text:
For 100k+ restartable work, SqliteArtifactStore gives indexed replay lookup and reopening without decoding history; JSONL remains right for portable, human-readable audit trails. The full comparison and durability semantics live in Results, Artifacts, and Resume.

Checkpoint batching trades result-publication latency for throughput: a result is yielded only after its transaction commits, so each item pays up to commit_interval_seconds (default 0.01 s) of batching delay on top of the commit itself.

docs.title: Restart workflow
docs.text:
1. Run with an artifact store and resume=ResumePolicy.REUSE_SUCCESSES.
  2. On crash or controlled stop (deadline, fail-fast, token/cost budget), fix the cause.
  3. Re-run the same source with a fresh store instance on the same path (a run closes its store when it finishes, so an instance can't be reused). Compatible successes replay without provider calls; failures and never-accepted items execute normally.
  4. Replayed items carry replayed_from_artifact=True; live token stats exclude their historical usage.

docs.title: Resource limits
docs.text:
• File descriptors: each worker's HTTP connection, the artifact database, its WAL/SHM sidecars, and your sink's outputs all consume descriptors — check RLIMIT_NOFILE per the production checklist.
  • Disk: the artifact grows with record count and payload size (the WAL stays at a bounded plateau during healthy writes). Budget from a measured bytes-per-record on your own payloads, not from anyone else's numbers.
  • Memory: framework memory stays bounded under the pattern above; the on-disk database intentionally grows, and anything your sink retains is yours.

docs.title: Verify with the scale harness
docs.text:
The repository ships a deterministic, credential-free harness (benchmarks/scale_soak) that drives these exact code paths — bounded streaming, slow consumers, 429 waves, retry mixes, stop/resume, the SQLite backend, and mixed RPM+TPM reservation/reconciliation — with exact item accounting and resource assertions:

make scale-smoke     # reduced CI-sized regression, ~15 s
make scale-100k      # reference profile, minutes
make scale-1m        # large-scenario subset, long

See Benchmarks for what each report proves and — just as important — what it does not: fake-provider throughput is not live-provider performance, local TPM smoothing is not GPU/KV-cache scheduling, and no million-item claim is made without a completed 1m report. The v0.22 dated evidence records exactly which 100k and 1m scenarios were completed on the release-candidate behavior.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
llm-minder logs through Python's standard logging module. Every logger is named after its module and sits under the llm_minder parent (for example llm_minder.parallel or llm_minder._internal.item_executor), so configuring logging.getLogger("llm_minder") controls all of them.

Logs are for people reading a run. Their wording isn't part of the API (see API stability); for anything a program consumes, use observers and events, get_stats(), or the returned BatchResult.

docs.title: What you see by default
docs.text: The library adds no handlers of its own. If your application never configures logging, Python's fallback handler prints WARNING and above to stderr, without timestamps or logger names. That means retry warnings and terminal failures appear even in a script that never mentions logging, while progress lines (INFO) and detail (DEBUG) don't.

docs.title: What each level shows
docs.text: Level What's logged ERROR Mostly items that failed for good, plus a few problems that don't end an item: an attempt that hit attempt_timeout (logged even when a retry then succeeds), a failing error classifier, a post-processor that failed or timed out, a failed cleanup step, and a cost function that raises or returns an invalid value, stopping the run. A terminal failure gets a traceback only when it's unexpected: logic_error, a failing classifier, an unclassified exception, or a non-retryable error raised by your own code rather than a provider SDK. Within one process_prompts()/process_stream() run, repeated terminal failures of the same kind (category, exception type and the first 200 characters of the message) are logged at ERROR once, then at DEBUG, and the run ends with one ERROR summary per repeated kind, such as "40 items failed with the same error: …". After 1,000 distinct kinds, further new kinds are logged at ERROR each time with no summary. call(), call_result() and LLMCallPool don't deduplicate. WARNING A retry ("Attempt 1/3 failed for item_7: … Retrying in 1.8s"); a rate limit that starts the shared cooldown ("Pausing all workers for 60.0s"); a progress callback that failed or timed out; a configuration value that was adjusted; and problems writing checkpoints, reading an artifact file's damaged tail, closing clients, or extracting response metadata. INFO A progress line every ProcessorConfig.progress_interval items (default 10) with throughput, tokens and error counts; the fallback progress line when progress=True is used without tqdm installed; a server-suggested cooldown raising the configured one; Gemini cache creation, reuse, renewal and deletion. DEBUG Per-attempt and lifecycle detail, and, within a batch or stream run, repeats of terminal failures already logged once at ERROR.

docs.title: Quieter output
docs.text:
Hide retries, cooldowns and progress, and keep errors:

import logging

logging.getLogger("llm_minder").setLevel(logging.ERROR)

ERROR isn't only terminal failures (see the table): an attempt timeout is logged even if the retry succeeds. For an exact record of which items failed, read the results (result.success, batch.failed) or an observer's ITEM_FAILED events rather than the log.

Use logging.CRITICAL to silence the library's logging entirely, for example in CI jobs that check the returned BatchResult instead. Retries still happen; they just aren't logged. Python warnings, such as the library's DeprecationWarnings, go through the warnings module rather than logging, so a log level doesn't hide them.

docs.title: More detail
docs.text:
Configure a handler (here, the root one) and lower the library's level:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")
logging.getLogger("llm_minder").setLevel(logging.INFO)  # or logging.DEBUG

INFO adds progress lines and cooldown detail; DEBUG adds per-attempt detail and is best kept for diagnosing a specific problem on a small run.

To send the library's logs somewhere separate, attach a handler to the llm_minder logger and set propagate = False on it.

docs.title: Alternatives to logs
docs.text:
• A progress bar: process_prompts(..., progress=True) (install the progress extra for tqdm), or your own progress_callback.
  • A summary at the end: print(batch.summary()) reports items, retries, tokens and timing percentiles.
  • Structured, per-event data: an observer receives typed lifecycle events (item started, completed or failed, rate limits, cooldowns) with documented payloads, which is the right input for metrics or dashboards.

docs.title: OpenAI-Compatible High-Throughput Guide
docs.text: Use this configuration pattern for OpenAI (Responses or Chat Completions), DeepSeek, OpenRouter, and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints when throughput is high enough that connection pools, startup bursts, and timeout tails matter.

docs.title: Model-Owned Client
docs.text:
from_api_key(max_connections=N) lets llm-minder size and own the httpx client. The model advertises N, so execution attempts are admitted before attempt_timeout starts and never queue invisibly inside the transport.

from llm_minder import (
    DeepSeekModel,
    DeepSeekStrategy,
    ParallelBatchProcessor,
    ProcessorConfig,
    RateLimitConfig,
    RetryConfig,
    StartupRampConfig,
)

model = DeepSeekModel.from_api_key(
    "deepseek-v4-flash",
    thinking=False,
    max_connections=64,
    timeout=60.0,
    max_retries=0,  # already the from_api_key default; shown for clarity
)
strategy = DeepSeekStrategy(model)
config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=64,
    attempt_timeout=60.0,
    retry=RetryConfig(max_attempts=3, max_rate_limit_retries=20),
    rate_limit=RateLimitConfig(cooldown_seconds=30.0),
    startup_ramp=StartupRampConfig(
        initial_concurrency=4,
        concurrency_step=4,
        ramp_interval_seconds=1.0,
        max_concurrency=64,
        jitter_seconds=0.05,
    ),
)

async with ParallelBatchProcessor(config=config) as processor:
    ...

docs.title: DeepSeek Strict Structured Output
docs.text:
For schema-constrained output on deepseek-v4-flash, select DeepSeek's Responses API and pass either a Pydantic model class or JSON Schema mapping:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Verdict(BaseModel):
    valid: bool
    reason: str


model = DeepSeekModel.from_api_key(
    "deepseek-v4-flash",
    api_surface="responses",
    response_schema=Verdict,
    thinking=False,
    max_connections=64,
    max_retries=0,  # the from_api_key default
)
strategy = DeepSeekStrategy(model, generation_config={"max_tokens": 256})

The strategy returns Verdict instances automatically. Requests still pass through the same gateway/batch admission, retry, timing, and accounting path. Metadata and inferred artifact identity record the Responses surface plus a canonical schema hash, so a frozen Chat JSON-mode result or a result from a different schema cannot be reused accidentally.

llm-minder validates the surface and schema locally and passes model IDs through to DeepSeek for validation. See the provider Responses reference for available models. The deepseek extra requires OpenAI SDK 1.66.2 or newer; caller-supplied clients must expose callable responses.create. This does not add multimodal work-item support or an automatic surface fallback. If schema enforcement is unavailable, choose Chat Completions explicitly with json_mode=True and pydantic_json_parser(...). That fallback validates locally but cannot guarantee or repair malformed provider JSON.

Set max_workers to the amount of useful application concurrency and max_connections to the provider-call capacity. They are often equal. A larger worker count can still help when middleware or post-processing occupies workers; llm-minder will admit only the model's advertised capacity into strategy.execute().

docs.title: User-Supplied Client
docs.text:
llm-minder cannot resize or reliably inspect a caller-supplied AsyncOpenAI client's httpx pool. Configure the transport explicitly and declare the same capacity on ProcessorConfig:

import httpx
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from llm_minder import OpenAIModel, OpenAIStrategy, ProcessorConfig

http_client = httpx.AsyncClient(
    limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=32, max_keepalive_connections=32),
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=10, read=60, write=30, pool=10),
)
client = AsyncOpenAI(
    api_key="sk-...",
    http_client=http_client,
    max_retries=0,
)
model = OpenAIModel("gpt-6-luna", client)
strategy = OpenAIStrategy(model)
config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=100,
    max_provider_concurrency=32,
    attempt_timeout=60,
)

# The caller owns a directly supplied client.
await client.close()

docs.title: Timeout Layers
docs.text:
Layer Scope httpx connect/read/write/pool timeout One transport operation OpenAI SDK timeout One SDK request attempt_timeout One strategy.execute() attempt, after llm-minder admission Retry backoff and coordinated cooldown Outside attempt_timeout LLMCallPool submit_timeout Full caller wall time, including all waits/retries

Avoid multiplying hidden SDK retries by llm-minder retries. from_api_key() already sets SDK max_retries=0; do the same for a client you build yourself. That gives llm-minder complete attempt timing, classification, and failed-token accounting. If SDK retries remain enabled, treat one strategy.execute() as the outer attempt and size attempt_timeout for all SDK work inside it.

docs.title: Startup Ramp vs Cooldown
docs.text:
• Use StartupRampConfig when a cold endpoint or new connection pool is sensitive to an immediate burst. It starts at initial_concurrency and adds concurrency_step every ramp_interval_seconds until the lowest configured, advertised, or ramp maximum is reached.
  • Lower max_workers when the provider has a stable hard concurrency limit and extra application workers add no value.
  • Use RateLimitConfig for reactive behavior after a 429/quota response: one coordinated cooldown, followed by the existing post-cooldown slow-start.

Startup-ramp and provider-capacity wait occur before attempt_timeout. WorkItemResult.timing separates them from execution, cooldown, and backoff.

docs.title: Shared Call Pools
docs.text:
For request-serving applications, construct one long-lived LLMCallPool so all callers share capacity and cooldown state. Set max_pending for load shedding and submit_timeout for the end-to-end request budget:

from llm_minder import LLMCallPool

async with LLMCallPool(
    strategy,
    config=config,
    max_pending=100,
    submit_timeout=30,
) as pool:
    response = await pool.submit("Summarize this request")

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Inspect Corrective action Throughput plateaus below provider capacity max_connections, max_provider_concurrency, execution p95 Align pool/admission limits; raise only after measuring High admission p95, normal execution p95 admission_wait_* and startup-ramp wait Raise capacity if the provider allows it, or lower worker/pending load Framework execution timeouts Attempt timeout_category, execution/provider duration Raise per-attempt timeout or fix provider/client latency httpx pool timeouts with a custom client httpx.Limits, pool timeout, explicit llm-minder capacity Set max_provider_concurrency no higher than the httpx pool Initial 429/5xx burst First-attempt errors and startup timing Enable StartupRampConfig; do not confuse it with post-429 slow-start Repeated 429s after recovery Cooldown duration and rate-limit retry count Lower steady capacity/RPM or increase coordinated cooldown Long request tail in a service Pool admission and submit_timeout Bound max_pending; set an end-to-end submit budget

For the exact timing boundary, see the production checklist.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
Tuning knobs that matter when you move from a 10-item test to a real bulk run. Each item links to the deeper reference where one exists.

When a run is already failing or appears stuck, use the Troubleshooting and FAQ alongside this preflight list.

docs.title: 1. Concurrency (concurrency / max_workers)
docs.text:
LLM calls are I/O-bound, so concurrency is "how many calls in flight at once", not a CPU count. Do not use os.cpu_count().

Prefer the single concurrency=N knob. It sets max_workers and max_provider_concurrency to N and, for factory-built OpenAI-compatible models, sizes the connection pool too (see Choosing Your Limits). Set max_workers separately only when you want the framework wider or narrower than the provider; an explicit value wins.

Situation Starting point General I/O-bound (most providers) 5–10 Rate-limited / low-quota endpoint 3–5, lean on the coordinated cooldown High-concurrency provider (e.g. DeepSeek, self-hosted vLLM) 50–200 — with concurrency=N the pool is sized to match (below)

Throughput from added workers flattens out well before you exhaust sockets/fds, so raising max_workers past the point where you're latency-bound just adds contention. Measure with examples/benchmark_worker_overhead.py (no network).

docs.title: 2. Connection pool (max_connections) vs max_workers
docs.text:
With concurrency=N and a factory-built OpenAI-compatible model (llm("...") or from_api_key() without max_connections), the pool is sized for you: N connections, all kept alive, before the first request.

Otherwise the openai SDK default applies to OpenAIModel / OpenRouterModel / DeepSeekModel: 1000 connections, of which 100 are kept alive. Above 100 concurrent requests, extra connections are opened and torn down for each request (a fresh handshake per call). Above 1000, extra workers wait inside httpx for a connection; that wait counts against attempt_timeout but isn't reported as a capacity wait. When you set max_workers yourself, or want a pool size other than concurrency, set max_connections explicitly (it sets both the connection and keep-alive limits):

model = DeepSeekModel.from_api_key(
    "deepseek-v4-flash",
    max_connections=200,   # match your ProcessorConfig(max_workers=...)
)

Models built with from_api_key(max_connections=N) advertise that capacity to their strategy. ParallelBatchProcessor and LLMCallPool emit a UserWarning when max_workers > N; the shared executor holds excess attempts in llm-minder admission before strategy.execute() and before attempt_timeout starts. Matching values avoids unnecessary admission wait:

model = DeepSeekModel.from_api_key("deepseek-v4-flash", max_connections=32)
strategy = DeepSeekStrategy(model)
config = ProcessorConfig(max_workers=32)

llm-minder cannot reliably inspect a caller-supplied AsyncOpenAI/httpx transport, so models constructed directly with OpenAIModel(model, client) advertise unknown capacity and do not warn. Set max_provider_concurrency to protect a known custom-client limit:

config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=100,
    max_provider_concurrency=32,  # outside attempt_timeout
)

When both the config and strategy advertise a capacity, the lower value wins. Limits are scoped to the underlying model, so multiple ModelStrategy instances sharing one model also share one capacity semaphore.

See OpenAI integration → connection-pool sizing.

docs.title: 3. Open-file limit (RLIMIT_NOFILE)
docs.text: Each in-flight request holds a socket (a file descriptor). A high max_workers plus the connection pool plus your app's own fds can hit the OS open-file limit — OSError: [Errno 24] Too many open files. This bites hardest on macOS (default soft limit ~256). The processor emits a UserWarning at construction when max_workers is close to the soft limit; it does not raise the limit for you. Fix by raising it (ulimit -n 8192, or resource.setrlimit early in the process) or lowering max_workers. Full guidance: Troubleshooting → throughput and connection pools.

docs.title: 4. Timeout and concurrency semantics
docs.text:
attempt_timeout is per attempt, enforced via asyncio.wait_for around each execute() — it is not a total budget across retries. With retry.max_attempts=3, a single item can spend up to ~3 × attempt_timeout in calls, plus backoff waits.

The timeout boundary is deliberately narrow:

Phase Counts against attempt_timeout? Batch queue wait / streaming backpressure No Worker or shared-call semaphore admission No Provider-capacity admission No Coordinated cooldown / post-cooldown slow-start No Proactive RPM/TPM quota wait No strategy.execute() Yes httpx pool wait occurring inside strategy.execute() Yes Retry backoff between attempts No

The transport-pool row is the common trap: llm-minder cannot distinguish provider time from a lower-level wait once strategy.execute() begins. Advertised or explicit capacity prevents that hidden wait by gating attempts first:

# Safe: 100 workers may do middleware/post-processing, but only 32 attempts
# enter strategy.execute() at once.
model = DeepSeekModel.from_api_key("deepseek-v4-flash", max_connections=32)
config = ProcessorConfig(max_workers=100, attempt_timeout=30)

Aligning the worker count avoids admission queues when the extra workers provide no other benefit:

model = DeepSeekModel.from_api_key("deepseek-v4-flash", max_connections=32)
config = ProcessorConfig(max_workers=32, attempt_timeout=30)

Rate limits are exempt from max_attempts (a 429 is "wait and retry", not a failed attempt — see below), so a throttled item can sit through many cooldowns without consuming its attempt budget. Bound that separately with retry.max_rate_limit_retries (default 20). Net: size attempt_timeout for one slow call, and use the two retry budgets to bound total effort.

ProcessorConfig(
    attempt_timeout=60.0,          # per attempt
    retry=RetryConfig(
        max_attempts=3,              # content/transport failures
        max_rate_limit_retries=20,   # throttling retries (separate budget)
    ),
)

For LLMCallPool, semaphore wait is outside attempt_timeout, while submit_timeout wraps the full caller path: both admission waits, cooldown, all attempts, and backoff. Use submit_timeout for an end-to-end request latency budget and attempt_timeout for one provider attempt.

Each WorkItemResult.admission_wait_seconds reports cumulative provider-capacity wait across attempts. get_stats() exposes total/max item wait, and MetricsObserver exposes attempt-level count, sum, max, and average wait, and can export them for Prometheus. WorkItemResult.timing further separates execution, built-in provider-call, cooldown, retry-backoff, and startup-ramp time for every physical try. Processor stats retain the latest 10,000 attempt samples and report admission and execution p50, p95, and p99 values.

docs.title: 5. Rate-limit configuration
docs.text:
When one worker hits a rate limit (HTTP 429 or an equivalent such as RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, error_category="rate_limit"), the framework runs a coordinated cooldown — all workers pause, then slow-start back up — instead of each worker hammering a throttled endpoint. Overload (503) and other 5xx errors use per-item retry backoff instead. Billing and daily-quota exhaustion (insufficient_balance, quota_exhausted) fail without retry; see ErrorCategory. Tune the cooldown via RateLimitConfig:

Field What it does cooldown_seconds Base pause after a rate limit (a server Retry-After raises it as a floor) backoff_multiplier Grows the cooldown on consecutive rate limits slow_start_items / slow_start_initial_delay / slow_start_final_delay Ramp delays as workers resume after a cooldown max_cooldown_seconds Cap on the escalated cooldown (default 600s)

Pair with proactive limiting (ProcessorConfig(max_requests_per_minute=...)) to stay under quota before you trip a 429 at all.

For cold-start burst protection, configure StartupRampConfig separately. It limits initial concurrency and raises it by a fixed step on each interval; unlike the fields above, it applies before the first provider call and does not require a preceding rate limit. Ramp wait remains outside attempt_timeout.

See the OpenAI-compatible high-throughput guide for owned/custom client recipes and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 6. Token-aware admission
docs.text:
Before enabling max_tokens_per_minute, verify all of the following:

  • Identify the provider/account that owns the quota and intentionally share a stable quota_scope across every strategy spending that budget.
  • Keep independent account quotas in distinct scopes. Do not use a credential, credential-derived string, or arbitrary repr() as a scope label.
  • Use a provider tokenizer where possible and measure estimator accuracy on representative small, medium, and large prompts.
  • Reserve expected output as well as input. Check that the largest single estimate fits inside max_tokens_per_minute.
  • Monitor refunded_tokens, underestimated_tokens, unknown_usage_attempts, and known_zero_usage_attempts; sustained debt means the estimate is too low.
  • Confirm whether an upstream gateway retries internally and whether it reports aggregate usage. Hidden attempts cannot be reconstructed by llm-minder.
  • Test one recoverable failed-usage retry, one unknown-usage timeout/transport failure, and cancellation both before and after provider start.
  • Verify replay and dry-run emit no quota events and do not consume live admission state.
  • Know that configuration failures (token_estimator_required, token_estimation_error, token_estimate_exceeds_limit, quota_scope_error) are never replayed on resume; fix the configuration and they re-execute. See configuration failures.

See Token-Aware Admission for reservation, reconciliation, FIFO, and visibility semantics.

docs.title: 7. Bounded streaming for large inputs
docs.text:
For a very large (or unbounded) input, don't buffer all the work up front. Use streaming mode with bounded max_queue_size and max_result_queue_size: workers run while you feed, so full queues apply backpressure instead of deadlocking or accumulating work in proportion to input size.

from llm_minder import ProcessorConfig, process_stream

config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=50,
    max_queue_size=200,
    max_result_queue_size=100,
)

async for result in process_stream(strategy, huge_prompt_source, config=config):
    if result.success:
        await save(result.item_id, result.output)   # completion order

huge_prompt_source can be any sync or async iterable (e.g. a generator reading a file lazily). The low-level equivalent is processor.start() / add_work() / finish() / results().

process_prompts() retains every result in its returned BatchResult, and process_all() requires work to be added before workers start. Neither is a bounded-memory result path for an unbounded workload. process_stream() avoids retaining results itself; set max_result_queue_size so a slow consumer applies backpressure to provider workers instead of accumulating completed items. See Bounded Work and Backpressure for incremental database input, low-level streaming, and separate input/output/provider/shared-call limits.

docs.title: 8. Single calls and the shared call pool (request paths)
docs.text:
For a web service's request path — where work arrives one call at a time, not as a batch — use LLMCallPool instead of standing up a processor per request:

  • One long-lived pool per app. Create it once at startup (e.g. a FastAPI lifespan handler) and share it across all request handlers. A single pool means one shared rate-limit cooldown — when one caller hits a 429, all callers briefly pause and then slow-start, instead of a thundering herd.
  • Set max_pending and submit_timeout for web paths. max_pending caps how many requests may wait beyond the max_workers running ones (total in flight ≤ max_workers + max_pending), so an overload sheds load instantly (rejecting with a failed result) rather than growing an unbounded waiter list; submit_timeout bounds per-caller latency so a request stuck behind a cooldown returns instead of hanging the handler. Both are off by default.
  • Do not create unbounded outer tasks. max_pending bounds pool admission, but one large asyncio.gather() still materializes every caller task. Use the bounded batch pattern for ingestion jobs or an explicitly bounded task window.
  • Shutdown drains admitted requests. aclose() (the async with exit) stops accepting new work, then waits for already-admitted requests to finish before cleaning up the shared strategy, so in-flight calls aren't cut off mid-flight. Set submit_timeout to bound how long shutdown waits for that drain; with no timeout it waits as long as the admitted work takes.

For a single ad-hoc call, call() / call_result() run one prompt through the same resilience pipeline with no pool at all.

docs.title: 9. Spend limits
docs.text: Set GuardrailConfig(max_total_tokens=...) on large or unattended runs, and max_total_cost with your own cost_function when a dollar ceiling matters. Caps are soft: calls already running when the cap is reached can overshoot it by at most one call per worker, so pair a cap with a per-call output limit (max_tokens) if the overshoot must stay small. The budget API is provisional and may change in a minor release (API stability). See Token and cost budgets.

docs.title: Prompt-cache hit rate
docs.text: A cache that stops hitting raises cost without failing any call. Watch the per-group cache_groups statistics, and on unattended runs set GuardrailConfig(min_cache_hit_rate=...) to stop when a group's recent hit rate drops. Long-lived LLMCallPools report the same statistics through pool.cache_stats(). See Prompt caching.

docs.title: 10. Cleanup
docs.text: Use the processor as an async with context manager so workers, caches, and HTTP clients are released. If you can't, call await processor.shutdown() when done.

docs.title: 11. Artifact storage (checkpoint/resume runs)
docs.text:
• Backend choice. JSONL for portable, human-inspectable audit logs; SqliteArtifactStore for 100k+ restartable runs needing indexed replay. See the comparison table.
  • Disk space and sidecars. Budget from a measured bytes-per-record on your payloads. SQLite runs also create -wal/-shm sidecar files next to the database; the WAL plateaus during healthy writes and is truncated on clean close (an -shm file may harmlessly remain).
  • Durability mode. SqliteDurability.BALANCED (default) survives process crashes; a power failure can lose recently committed transactions. Choose FULL when power-loss durability matters more than write throughput. Neither mode encrypts the file — use filesystem permissions and volume encryption for sensitive outputs.
  • Commit batch latency. Results are published only after their transaction commits; commit_interval_seconds (default 0.01 s) is added result latency. Lower it for latency-sensitive streaming, raise the batch size for maximum append throughput.
  • Write permissions. The store creates parent directories and needs write access for the database and its sidecars.
  • Single-writer deployment. One writable store instance per artifact file, in one process. Sequential reopen is supported; concurrent external readers obey busy_timeout_seconds. There is no distributed work claiming or cross-process exactly-once execution.
  • Before million-item claims. Run make scale-100k (and scale-1m for seven digits) on a representative environment and review the report — don't extrapolate from profile existence. See Benchmarks.

docs.title: Prompt caching: getting hits and keeping them
docs.text:
A prompt cache that stops hitting doesn't make any call fail. It makes every call cost more, sometimes several times more, and nothing in the results says so unless you look. This guide covers how to get cache hits, how to see them per job, and how to stop a run, or alert, when they drop.

The statistics, the floor and CacheGroupTracker are provisional: new in 0.30, and they may change in a minor release (API stability). For the exact rules, see Cache hit-rate floor.

A runnable, credential-free walkthrough of everything below is in examples/example_prompt_caching.py.

docs.title: 1. Get cache hits
docs.text:
Every supported provider caches a prompt prefix. Put the static part first and the per-item part last:

  • Put long instructions, examples and reference text in system_instruction (or a system message), and only the item in the prompt.
  • Keep the static part byte-for-byte identical across calls. A timestamp, a shuffled example list or an item id near the start makes every prefix unique.
  • Prefer a separate system instruction to one user message that joins static instructions to per-item data. How much of such a message a provider can reuse depends on the provider and model: a static prefix at its start can still hit (DeepSeek caches any shared prefix, and OpenAI models before GPT-5.6 cache at fixed token intervals), but anything per-item early in it makes every prompt unique from that point on.

Providers also need a minimum prefix length before they cache anything; for OpenAI it is 1,024 tokens on GPT-5.6 and later and depends on request settings for earlier models (OpenAI's prompt caching guide). Provider specifics: OpenAI, Anthropic (cache_control= turns on automatic caching), OpenRouter (including Anthropic's opt-in cache_control markers), and Gemini (GeminiCachedModel for explicit context caching).

docs.title: 2. What each provider supports
docs.text:
The statistics and the floor work with any strategy. Each call needs cached-token counts in its usage (cached_input_tokens, and cache_write_input_tokens where the provider reports writes) and a group label in its metadata (cache_group).

Built-in model Cached tokens counted Group set automatically cache_group= label OpenAIModel yes prompt_cache_key, else a system-instruction hash yes OpenRouterModel yes, when the upstream reports them prompt_cache_key, else a system-instruction hash yes DeepSeekModel yes, from DeepSeek's cache-hit field system-instruction hash (DeepSeek takes no key) yes GeminiModel yes system-instruction hash yes AnthropicModel yes, reads and writes system-instruction hash yes GeminiCachedModel yes a stable hash of the cached content yes PydanticAIStrategy yes none (calls count as ungrouped) no Custom strategy or CallableStrategy if your usage reports them your metadata["cache_group"] n/a

Two features are OpenAI-specific:

  • prompt_cache_key on OpenAIModel and OpenRouterModel. On OpenAI models before GPT-5.6 it routes calls that share a key toward the same cache; on GPT-5.6 and later OpenAI routes automatically and the key only separates cache accounting. DeepSeek's and Gemini's caches take no key.
  • Miss reasons. OpenAI's Responses API can explain a miss (prompt_cache_diagnostics); the reason becomes the call's cache_miss_reason. Other providers don't explain misses, so last_miss_reason stays None unless your strategy sets it.

docs.title: 3. Name your cache groups
docs.text:
Statistics and the floor are kept per cache group: the calls that should share a cache. A built-in model picks a group for you (table above), but a label you choose reads better and keeps jobs apart:

from llm_minder import DeepSeekModel, OpenAIModel

# A label for every call this model makes. It is never sent to the provider.
model = DeepSeekModel.from_api_key("deepseek-v4-flash", cache_group="tier1-dedupe")

# OpenAI: send a cache key on every call; it also names the group. (On GPT-5.6
# and later the key separates cache accounting; earlier models also route by it.)
model = OpenAIModel.from_api_key(
    "gpt-6-luna",
    system_instruction=LONG_STATIC_INSTRUCTIONS,
    prompt_cache_key="classify-v3",  # or "auto": a hash of the system instruction
)

A strategy can override the model's label with OpenAIStrategy(model, generation_config={"cache_group": "..."}) (any built-in model strategy takes generation_config), and a custom execute() can pass config={"cache_group": "..."} to model.generate() for one call. The order is: a metadata extractor's cache_group, then the per-call label, then the model's label, then the cache key, then the system-instruction hash.

Calls with none of these share one ungrouped bucket (group is None), which the floor also checks. Two unrelated keyless jobs in one run land in that bucket together, so label them.

For a custom strategy or CallableStrategy, put the group in the metadata you return:

from llm_minder import CallOutcome

async def invoke(prompt, *, attempt, timeout, state):
    response = await client.generate(prompt)
    return CallOutcome(
        output=response.text,
        token_usage={
            "input_tokens": response.usage.input_tokens,
            "output_tokens": response.usage.output_tokens,
            "cached_input_tokens": response.usage.cache_read_tokens,
        },
        metadata={"cache_group": "extract-v2"},
    )

One hot key (OpenAI models before GPT-5.6). On these models a cache lives on one machine, and OpenAI's guide suggests about 15 requests per minute in total for each key; busier traffic overflows to other machines and caches less well. With many workers on one key, split the key (for example classify-v3-0 through classify-v3-3, chosen per item) and give the models one cache_group label so they report together, or leave the labels apart to compare the shards. GPT-5.6 and later route automatically, so there is no need to split keys for them.

docs.title: 4. Read the statistics
docs.text:
Every processor run keeps per-group statistics, with or without a floor:

async with ParallelBatchProcessor[None, str, None](config=config) as processor:
    ...
    result = await processor.process_all()
    stats = await processor.get_stats()

for group in stats["cache_groups"]:  # most input tokens first
    print(group["group"], f"{group['hit_rate']:.0%}", group["last_miss_reason"])

Each entry has measured_calls, unmeasured_calls, input_tokens, cached_input_tokens, cache_write_input_tokens, the cumulative hit_rate (cached over input tokens), window_hit_rate over the group's last cache_hit_window measured calls, and last_miss_reason. The BATCH_COMPLETED observer event carries the same lists. Calls without usage (or with no input tokens) count as unmeasured_calls and never move a rate.

Run-wide totals are on the result: result.total_cached_tokens, result.total_cache_write_tokens and result.cache_hit_rate (a percentage, 0-100, unlike the per-group rates, which are fractions).

The ceiling isn't 100%. The hit rate counts every input token, and the per-item part is never cached. A 2,000-token static prefix with 100-token items tops out at about 95%, and a group's first call, which writes the cache, reads 0%.

docs.title: 5. Stop a run when hits drop
docs.text:
from llm_minder import GuardrailConfig, ProcessorConfig

config = ProcessorConfig(
    max_workers=20,
    guardrails=GuardrailConfig(
        min_cache_hit_rate=0.7,
        cache_hit_window=50,
    ),
)

Once a group has cache_hit_window measured calls, a window hit rate below min_cache_hit_rate stops the run like configurable fail-fast. Check for it on the result:

from llm_minder import ErrorCategory

if result.termination.error_category == ErrorCategory.CACHE_HIT_RATE_BELOW_FLOOR:
    print(result.termination.reason)
    # "Cache hit rate for group 'classify' fell to 57.1% over the last 50
    #  measured calls (floor 70.0%); last miss reason: input_changed"

Calls that hadn't started end batch_aborted, and abort_mode decides what happens to calls already running. The resumed run starts with fresh statistics.

What a rerun can reuse depends on the fix. With an artifact store and ResumePolicy.REUSE_SUCCESSES, a fix that changes only cache routing, such as a cache key or label, leaves completed items compatible, so they replay and only the rest are called. A fix that changes what the model is asked, however, needs care in both directions. A changed item prompt changes the item's fingerprint, so completed items run again. A change outside the item prompt, such as the system instruction or other request settings, may not be part of the compatibility check, so old outputs can replay unless you change the store's ArtifactIdentity or bump prompt_version (see Results and artifacts).

Choosing the values.

  • Floor: set it below your ceiling (section 4) with room for noise, and above the rate a broken cache gives. If a working job reads 90% and a broken one 0%, 0.7 catches the break without false alarms. Measure a healthy run first, using the statistics without a floor.
  • Window: it is also the warm-up, because no group is checked until its window is full. Make it comfortably larger than max_workers: calls that start together before the cache is written all miss. Larger windows react later but trip less on noise. The default is 50.
  • Many groups: each group has its own window, so a small group may never be checked. A run tracks at most 64 groups; with a floor set, a 65th group stops the run, because the floor can't be enforced for groups it doesn't track.

The floor applies to processor runs only. call(), call_result() and LLMCallPool reject it; check a pool yourself (next section).

docs.title: 6. Long-lived pools and resumed jobs
docs.text:
LLMCallPool keeps the same per-group statistics, without a floor:

stats = pool.cache_stats()  # same shape as get_stats(); always includes window_hit_rate
pool.reset_cache_stats()  # start counting again, e.g. after deploying a new prompt

The cumulative hit_rate of a long-lived pool moves slowly, so watch window_hit_rate, or check a floor yourself with the pool's tracker:

for breach in pool.cache_tracker.below_floor(0.7):
    logger.warning(breach.message)  # the same message a processor run would stop with

To keep the statistics across a restart, save the tracker and pass the restored one to the next pool:

import json

from llm_minder import CacheGroupTracker, LLMCallPool

saved = json.dumps(pool.cache_tracker.to_dict())  # at a checkpoint or on shutdown

# Next process:
tracker = CacheGroupTracker.from_dict(json.loads(saved))
pool = LLMCallPool(strategy, config=config, cache_tracker=tracker)

The saved state includes every group's window, so the restored tracker continues exactly, warm-up included. A restored tracker keeps its own window, whatever cache_hit_window the new config sets.

Without saved state, rebuild a tracker from saved results:

tracker = CacheGroupTracker(window=50)
for row in saved_results:  # WorkItemResult objects
    tracker.record_result(row)

This reads lower than the live statistics did when retries were billed. A result's token_usage adds up every attempt of its item, failed ones included, while live tracking counts only the attempt that returned. Failed results are skipped.

CacheGroupTracker also works on its own, outside the framework: tracker.record(group, usage, miss_reason=...) counts one call, with the same rules. A tracker isn't thread-safe; use it from one event loop or thread.

docs.text:
